SK1043 The for loop is a while

A for with no initializer and no incrementor is a while written with two empty clauses.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS1264

Why

for promises a bound and then declares none, so a reader has to check both semicolons to find out there is nothing in them. The rewrite is exact rather than merely equivalent: with no incrementors, continue jumps to the condition in both forms, and nothing else in a for is being used.

Example

Instead of:

for (; !reader.EndOfStream;) {
    Consume(reader.ReadLine());
}

Write:

while (!reader.EndOfStream) {
    Consume(reader.ReadLine());
}

When it does not fire

for (;;) is deliberately not reported: it is the idiomatic infinite loop, and while (true) says nothing the original did not. A declaration, an initializer or an incrementor in any clause excludes the loop — converting a for (int i = 0; c;) would have to lift the declaration into the enclosing scope, which is a different rewrite with a different risk. Comments and preprocessor directives inside the empty clauses exclude it too, because the fix replaces the whole header.
